Diegograndi Special Coverage / Global 21 September 2026 7 minutes Updates from the UN General Assembly 2026 Marking the opening of the 81st UN General Assembly, Crisis Group experts discuss challenges facing the UN’s efforts to promote international peace and security. This page includes updates from the High-Level Week in New York and recent Crisis Group coverage of the UN. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy World leaders are gathering in New York during the week of 21 September for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. They will find an organisation trapped in an open-ended institutional crisis. UN diplomacy to halt wars and ease civilian suffering is largely paralysed, while a second year of cost cutting has weakened the organisation’s capacity to respond. The UN is in need of revival. Even with these limitations, the UN remains the only universal forum for international cooperation on war and peace, even as the world order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope that the next Secretary-General, set to be selected by the end of 2026, can help the organisation forge a new direction that enhances diplomacy and deepens respect for international law. A new Secretary-General, regardless of the skills and experiences that she or he may bring to the role, cannot solve the world’s crises overnight. But she or he can and should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capacities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. titre: Somalia Awaits a New Security Order as Mission Drawdown Looms
resume: Somalia Awaits a New Security Order as Mission Drawdown Looms pfranz Fri, 09/18/2026 - 21:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Somali police officers walk along a road median while patrolling a busy street in Mogadishu, on November 10, 2025. TONY KARUMBA / AFP Commentary / Africa 18 September 2026 16 minutes Somalia Awaits a New Security Order as Mission Drawdown Looms The multilateral missions that have helped the Somali government fight Al-Shabaab for nearly two decades may be coming to an end. Mogadishu and its partners should get started now developing a plan for what they will do next. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Somalia The multilateral missions that have protected Somalia’s government from the jihadist insurgent group Al-Shabaab since 2007 could be drawing to a close. In early July, the U.S. informed the African Union (AU) that it would not back an extension of the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) – which provides crucial logistical assistance to the AU’s Support and Stabilisation Mission – beyond the end of its current mandate in December. The U.S. position has subsequently softened, with U.S. diplomats telling the AU in September that Washington would consider a twelve-month extension before calling a stop to further UN aid. This development buys time for a more orderly drawdown or some kind of transition. But the reality remains inescapable: the security blanket that Somalia has lived under for almost two decades is on borrowed time. The forthcoming UN General Assembly provides a prime opportunity for the Somali government, the AU and its security partners to kickstart essential discussions about how to keep Somalia safe. Given the AU mission’s reliance on the UN to provide water, food, fuel and transport, it will almost certainly be unable to continue in anything like its present form without UN help. The AU, its foreign partners and the Somali federal government are considering how to keep the mission going, but they do not have any particularly enticing options in mind. There is no clear alternative to the UN office, whose budget is nearly half a billion dollars, when it comes to setting up, running and paying for a multinational force. That said, predictions that the prospective end of UN and possibly AU security assistance will see the government collapse and Al-Shabaab emerge victorious are wide of the mark. While Al-Shabaab remains a major threat to the Somali government and controls swathes of southern and central Somalia, the group is largely confined to rural areas. The government’s grip extends to most urban centres, with security in the capital Mogadishu improving sharply in recent years. Support from the UN has helped maintain this precarious status quo. But an end to multilateral assistance need not culminate in the federal state’s downfall, even if a mismanaged transition could spell trouble. A combination of Somali and other international forces, including those already stationed in the country, should form part of a new international security structure. It is now up to Mogadishu and its international partners to begin planning this shift before it is too late. Approximate areas of operation for AUSSOM troop contributors. Some troop contributors maintain bilateral contingents in addition to their AUSSOM deployments. Source: Crisis Group research as of September 2026. CRISIS GROUP More Trouble for a Struggling Mission The AU mission and its UN logistics support office – the mainstay of foreign assistance for Somalia’s security – rely on troops from Africa and funds from farther afield. Ugandan troops were the first to be deployed upon the mission’s launch in 2007, followed soon thereafter by forces from Burundi and Djibouti. Kenya and Ethiopia joined in 2012 and 2014, respectively, after first launching their own bilateral interventions to safeguard their borders from Al-Shabaab incursions. The mission pushed the jihadist group out of many urban centres in south-central Somalia in the 2010s, including Mogadishu in 2011. More recently, however, the AU has struggled to find money for the mission, with long-time donors like the EU whittling down their contributions and pushing for the exit door. The mission has been running a large deficit for several years, even as it has taken measures to cut spending. Troop numbers have dwindled from 22,000 in the mid-2010s to around 12,000 today. Instead of launching offensive operations deep in the hinterlands controlled by Al-Shabaab, the mission has turned more toward protecting urban areas it already holds, while playing a supporting role in Somali army campaigns. The financial crunch has since extended to the UN’s logistical support, funded through UN assessed contributions – mandatory dues paid by all member states to underwrite the global body’s operations. Even before the Trump administration took office, U.S. officials were wary of the model that sees UN finances flow to a non-UN mission, regarding it as an undesirable precedent. In early 2025, the U.S. blocked a proposal for the AU mission to also receive funding through UN assessed contributions, arguing in part that the UN is already spending heavily on UNSOS. In September 2025, the U.S. shelved planned contributions to the UN peacekeeping budget, including for UNSOS. Hence, its refusal to support the office’s existence any further does not come as a complete surprise. Much as Washington has no wish to see an Al-Shabaab resurgence, it seems to be pulling the plug on a setup that has done much to keep the group in check. Much as Washington has no wish to see an Al-Shabaab resurgence, it seems to be pulling the plug on a setup that has done much to keep the group in check. Despite this apparent contradiction, the U.S. government believes that the status quo is no longer tenable: the multilateral missions are not as effective as they once were, while the Somali government should bear the primary responsibility for leading the fight with Al-Shabaab. U.S. diplomats believe that Somali elites are skirting their duties, preoccupied with pursuing political vendettas rather than combating jihadists. It is difficult to know if President Donald Trump’s evident personal animus toward Somalia has also played a role. A number of U.S. officials agree that ending UNSOS, and by extension threatening the existence of the AU mission, is a risk. It was probably for this reason that the U.S. backtracked in September to grant the UN mission an additional twelve months to draw down. But this move only defers rather than eliminates the challenges ahead. The U.S. argues that Mogadishu can keep Al-Shabaab at bay by enhancing the deployment of Somali forces, and combining this measure with assistance from abroad, including troops from neighbouring countries and air support from the U.S. and Türkiye. The U.S. says it remains ready to contribute to fighting Al-Shabaab. It just no longer wants to do so through a multilateral vehicle that it regards as an unnecessary expense. Are There Alternatives to UNSOS? The drawdown and eventual closure of UNSOS would, in effect, mean that the AU mission could not continue as currently designed. The UN mission keeps AU troops supplied with food, water and fuel, sustaining nearly 50 bases across southern Somalia. It also provides transport for AU deployments. When funds permit, it supports Somali soldiers operating alongside the AU personnel. Privately, AU officials say the mission cannot continue without UN support: one termed the U.S. decision on the UNOSOS mandate “life-threatening”. Even with a twelve-month stay of execution, the UN support office’s coming year will be focused on winding down its extensive logistical responsibilities. Deciding what comes next has become imperative for the Somali authorities. A few options for logistical assistance for the AU mission have been mooted, but all face serious drawbacks. In July, the Somali government, the AU and troop-contributing states met in the Ugandan capital Kampala to discuss the mission’s future. They endorsed a plan for uninterrupted support for another eighteen to 24 months, a period that would be used to carry out offensives against Al-Shabaab and a more gradual drawdown. For Washington, however, an extension of UN support beyond what is now on the table is out of the question, a stance it communicated in September. Another option would be for the AU to use the time UNSOS has left to replace it with an AU logistical mission. Another option would be for the AU to use the time UNSOS has left to replace it with an AU logistical mission. But given the AU’s lack of experience in running such a complex operation, this option appears unworkable in the near term. The AU could subcontract logistics to a private company, but diplomats note that it would take up to two years to establish a mission with capabilities similar to those of UNSOS. Even if it were possible, the financial crunch would not vanish. With the AU mission unable even to cover troop stipends, there is no way at present that it could shoulder the costs of logistics. The deeper pockets of partners alarmed by the possibility of an imminent worsening of Somali security, such as the EU or Gulf Arab countries, might be prised open to an extent. But with so many other crises competing for resources, a donor boost remains a long shot. Alternatively, the AU could take whatever funding is available from the EU and others, channelling it toward covering troop stipends and the logistics of a smaller mission. This option would enable the AU to maintain its presence, but only by sacrificing its operational clout, perhaps by retrenching at a few key locations, most likely in and around Mogadishu and regional capitals. But countries contributing troops to the AU mission already argue they do not have enough personnel to protect themselves, let alone undertake forward operations. Reducing their numbers further could end up at a point where the mission is unable to defend itself or others from Al-Shabaab attack. With limited funding committed for 2026 and nothing beyond that, the AU might also find it difficult to win donors over to the idea of supporting a less effective version of the same mission. A further variant of this option is being floated in Addis Ababa, where the AU has its headquarters: reconfiguring the mission under a new regional mechanism, but still with an AU mandate. In this scenario, many of the African troops deployed in Somalia would stay, but under a setup not unlike the Multinational Joint Task Force in the Lake Chad basin, a regional initiative to combat Boko Haram. Parallels with the Lake Chad basin are imperfect, however: the various national militaries operating there largely do so inside their own frontiers, coordinating more on cross-border matters. The proposal also offers little by way of a solution to the logistics and funding dilemmas, simply passing the buck to troop-contributing states. One or another of these options might emerge to enable Somalia’s multilateral security support to stagger on past 2027. The U.S. decision to grant an extra twelve months buys time to evaluate all the options and allows for less haste in the overhaul. But one way or another, a transition, with all its uncertainties, appears imminent. Turning to Somali Forces The AU’s exit strategy is premised on Somali forces standing ready to take the mission’s place when it finally shuts down. There is no doubt that the Somali National Army has boosted its strength in recent years, generating upward of 10,000 new troops under training schemes supported by foreign partners like Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates and Eritrea. But it is still ill-prepared to fully and rapidly take the AU mission’s place. Certain areas handed over by the mission to Somali forces in recent years have later fallen into Al-Shabaab’s hands. Even when the Somali army has led operations against Al-Shabaab, such as in Lower Shabelle in 2025-2026, it has remained dependent on external support. Somali officials have argued for many years that they can take full responsibility for security, but that they need more time. Many in the current government and its predecessors have wanted Somali forces to step up, only to find themselves hamstrung by political rifts within the federal system that have weakened the national security apparatus. State-level forces are generally underdeveloped, while the divisions between federal officials and leaders in Puntland and Jubaland, who are at loggerheads over how power and resources are divided in Somalia’s federal system, hinder the emergence of a unified national army. During times of political crisis, such as the election-related turmoil at present, federal and state forces sometimes turn their guns on each other. These shortcomings have driven Mogadishu to establish a series of bilateral security agreements with Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia, ensuring that their troops will stay despite the AU mission’s withdrawal. Uganda reportedly has a force of around 2,000 troops stationed in and around Mogadishu, while Kenya and Ethiopia retain larger contingents closer to their own borders. Bilateral foreign forces in Somalia have remained stable even as the AU mission shrinks, a trend that will probably continue after its eventual departure. What Could a New Security Approach Look Like? The AU mission’s future is for now unclear. While replacing support from the UN, and possibly finding a substitute for the mission, would undoubtedly be a huge undertaking, the situation is not hopeless. With proper planning, political leadership and a measure of continued foreign backing, the Somali government should be able to shift from dependence on a multilateral force to a series of bilateral relationships that prevent a major security breakdown and sweeping military gains by Al-Shabaab. That said, there is little doubt that the impending loss of the UN support office’s annual spending on Somali security needs will cause headaches. Even if the AU manages somehow to retain a presence, the most likely shape of Somalia’s future security support will derive chiefly from the deeply rooted interests of Mogadishu’s foreign partners. Key members of the AU mission, particularly Kenya and Ethiopia, are primarily motivated by border security, particularly the desire to maintain a buffer against Al-Shabaab. Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni views his country’s longstanding deployment as a key part of his legacy. He likely holds out hope that Mogadishu will be able to find a donor to pay for Ugandan units stationed around the capital. From outside the region, Türkiye has become Somalia’s most important bilateral partner in recent years, training thousands of Somali troops as well as deploying advanced military assets like drones and F-16s. Ankara also remains keen to protect its wide-ranging strategic investments in the country. The U.S., for its part, asserts that it will, for now, maintain its bilateral counter-terrorism operations, particularly its drone program. Making full use of these various bilateral arrangements is the most pragmatic way to go about preventing a serious deterioration in security after UNSOS closes. Making full use of these various bilateral arrangements is the most pragmatic way to go about preventing a serious deterioration in security after UNSOS closes, regardless of what happens to the AU mission, while buying more time for the Somali military to assume greater responsibility. The AU mission’s major troop contributors would ideally keep most of their contingents where they are, arranging their own logistics in the process, but changes are likely. The loss of UNSOS assistance will probably spur Kenya and Ethiopia into consolidating positions nearer their own borders, while Uganda will probably focus more on protecting Mogadishu and its environs. Smaller troop contributors like Burundi and Djibouti, on the other hand, may be less inclined to continue without additional support. In areas where foreign troops do withdraw, Somali forces should prepare to take over. Mogadishu claimed in early August that it has 14,000 troops available for military operations, who could instead be deployed as holding forces to take the place of departing AU personnel. Somali troops tend not to be as well trained or equipped as their AU counterparts, however, making a one-to-one switch from AU to Somali soldiers a hazardous proposition. Taking these steps might contain Al-Shabaab to its rural bastions and avoid the loss of major cities. Proper coordination with bilateral forces could help protect the most strategically important areas, including towns, infrastructure and supply routes. But a modest fallback from some of the positions that are now under the AU mission’s control seems inevitable. Uganda, for example, maintains more than a dozen bases in the Lower Shabelle region, which will be difficult to hold without UNSOS logistical support. Smaller towns surrounded by Al-Shabaab, such as Qoryoley, could be at risk of falling to the insurgents once the AU pulls out. Parts of Hirshabelle would also be vulnerable due to the concentration of Al-Shabaab forces in the area since 2025, adding pressure to towns along the main road in the state, such as Jalalaqsi. Even small losses could give momentum back to Al-Shabaab, while the capture of roads and economic centres would help sustain the group financially. It may be possible over the coming years to keep parts of the battlefield tilted in the Somali authorities’ favour through the calibrated deployment of foreign troops, especially when it comes to the defence of urban centres and transport arteries. Still, the systemic challenges to Somali security thrown up by a radical change in security arrangements cannot be wished away. If they are left unaddressed, the danger will rise of greater government losses and an Al-Shabaab surge outside its rural strongholds. First, shifting the security burden onto African states will not resolve the funding problem unless donors and Somali officials take bold steps. If the AU wants to remain involved, it will have to do more to raise its own funds. If not, the AU mission’s current backers – primarily the EU and UK, which in 2025 together contributed approximately $90 million – could find ways to transfer this support to cover logistics and stipends for troop-contributing states from the region and Somali forces. Gulf Arab states, which number among Somalia’s key backers, may even be more inclined to support bilateral forces, viewing multilateral support as a poor investment because it translates into minimal diplomatic influence. Even though its resources are strained, the Somali government could also reduce the burden on foreign donors: the government has managed to raise domestic revenue in recent years and has even funded a number of internal military operations and deployments. The more it can take on, the less it will need to lobby the same donors on behalf of other African troop contributors. Secondly, the Somali government, troop-contributing countries and donors will need a forum in which to debate the country’s security needs and priorities. Security coordination within the AU mission has often proven a challenge, but the mission’s guiding framework helped ensure that its contributors adhered to a basic common strategy. The government should now establish a new forum that would meet regularly to coordinate with its bilateral partners, enabling Mogadishu to impress upon them the country’s main security requirements and hopefully curbing the pursuit of individual interests by troop-contributing states. Somalia’s security partners in turn should focus on fulfilling their security roles and avoid meddling in local politics in their areas of operation. A forum could also be an opportunity for the government to detail a national plan for Somalia’s future security, which would help assuage local concerns that a transition might leave some parts of the country better protected than others. Without effective coordination, bilateral security relationships could hasten the country’s fragmentation by fracturing it into various zones of influence that overlap with Somalia’s current divisions between the federal authorities and assertive member states. Furthermore, there is a risk that powerful partners might look to Mogadishu to provide exclusive concessions – economic or otherwise – in return for military assistance. Better coordination with multiple partners will help the Somali authorities handle these demands and keep the focus on making the country safe. With negotiations on the AU mission’s next mandate set to kick off at the UN Security Council by December, Somalia would benefit greatly from having a plan and buy-in from security partners in place by then. What Should Happen Now? Somalia’s multilateral security system has been limping toward its finale for several years. Establishing a new model without the UN support office and possibly the AU mission will be arduous; a series of bilateral security relationships is unlikely to match what multilateral deployments have achieved. Current funding and geopolitical realities, however, make this shift the most realistic option beyond 2027. The government should be using the time it has to make this change work. A clear grasp of the challenges ahead would be a good place to start. Diplomats from some of Mogadishu’s security partners say both the government and the AU expect that further compromises can be hammered out over the future of UNSOS. If so, that confidence is misplaced. The Trump administration appears intent on seeing the end of the UN support mission, even if it has signalled that more time is available to allow for a smoother transition. It is also hard to gauge how much UNSOS will be able to do in 2027 as it focuses on its liquidation. Rather than assume business as usual, Mogadishu and its partners should use the temporary reprieve they have been granted to construct a new security system that can kick into action as early as the second half of 2027. The Somali government should urgently convene its security partners to establish a broad division of responsibilities and priorities to follow the departure of UNSOS. Setting out a viable plan for the country after UN support winds down also has a better chance of attracting fresh donor backing. A shift primarily to bilateral support is still a temporary measure, and it should only buy time for a lasting solution to the country’s troubles: a Somali government that can manage its own security needs. Mogadishu’s shortcoming in achieving this goal, despite two decades of foreign support, is rooted in entrenched political divisions rather than just financial and technical challenges. In the short term, the government should be ready to deploy troops to areas likely to be vacated by foreign troops; it should launch major new offensives only once the transition has been consolidated. But for the security transition to work over the long term, Somalia’s government and political class must address their political divisions and row in the same direction. They could start to do so by resolving the dispute regarding the timing and format for elections, continuing by concluding these polls swiftly so that an incoming administration with a clear mandate can take office. The new administration should make preparing for a security transition an overriding priority. It should lay out a plan for how Somali forces can take over from foreign troops, including by bringing federal member states into discussions regarding the future of Somali security. Such a plan is the best way to realise the country’s full sovereignty – an oft-stated ambition of the Somali government. But the longer political disputes drag on, the greater the risk that the transition to Somali forces falters and Al-Shabaab resurges. The U.S. decision to pull the plug on UNSOS appears to be a defining act in the decline of Somalia’s multilateral security system. In its aftermath, short-term gains by Al-Shabaab look inevitable. But a well-managed transition should help mitigate any losses and lay the groundwork for Somalia’s eventual stability. titre: Closing the New War Front in Yemen
resume: Closing the New War Front in Yemen cthuratong Fri, 09/18/2026 - 13:46 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Internally displaced (IDP) Yemenis who fled their homes due to renewed clashes between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the country's Houthi rebels drive to the safety of al-Kadah in the Taiz Governorate, southwestern Yemen on September 6, 2026. Ahmad Al-Basha / AFP Statement / Middle East & North Africa 18 September 2026 9 minutes Closing the New War Front in Yemen The Houthis’ rapid advance on the western Yemeni coast has opened a new front in the Middle East war that began with February’s U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran. A truce in Yemen is an urgent priority, so that hostilities do not spiral, drawing in more countries. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Yemen Saudi Arabia Iran In mid-September, Houthi rebels charged down Yemen’s western coast, seizing strategic territory from government-aligned forces and turning the country into an active front in the Middle East confrontation pitting the U.S. and Israel against Iran. Their rapid advance has also brought Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, squarely into the region-wide struggle, in which the Houthis side with Tehran . On 11 September, government-linked forces lost the coastal city of Mokha and much of the defensive system stretching from southern Hodeida through western Taiz toward Bab al-Mandab, upending the local military balance and putting the Houthis in a stronger position from which to attack the government’s principal ally, Saudi Arabia, and shipping in the Red Sea. The gains come as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is already bottled up by overlapping Iranian and U.S. restrictions, putting further pressure on world oil markets. The immediate priority should be to reach a truce. Oman, in particular, should use its channels to all sides to achieve a freeze in their positions: the Houthis would halt their escalation both inside Yemen, particularly around Taiz, and against Saudi Arabia; in return, Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government would cease all hostilities with the rebels. Iran, which may see benefit in another front heating up, is running considerable risk in further alienating its neighbours. Instead, it ought to use its leverage to push the Houthis in a conciliatory direction – a step it would be far more likely to take amid de-escalation with the U.S. along the lines of the memorandum of understanding, now defunct, reached in June. The next challenge will be to renew talks about a political settlement, backed by confidence-building steps concerning Sanaa airport and the Yemeni economy as well as by Iranian support for reciprocal Houthi restraint. The Houthis Gain a Strategic Foothold The Houthis’ offensive on the western coast marks yet another flare-up of Yemen’s conflict, as the rebels attempt to break a long-running stalemate with the internationally recognised government and its Saudi backers. The surge in fighting began with attacks on 20 July on Saudi territory and Saudi-linked ships in the Red Sea, before the Houthis launched a ground assault on government-aligned forces and seized the coastline. The Houthis had previously spent weeks probing the government’s defences. In August, they repeatedly struck the town of Mokha, as well as its port and nearby positions, with ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden boats, while attempting to infiltrate the front line in western Taiz. These preparatory attacks allowed them to identify key defensive positions, gauge reinforcement times and test how government-aligned formations would respond to simultaneous pressure. The decisive battle commenced when Houthi forces moved against the government’s supply lines near Mokha. Advances through the western mountains in Taiz, followed by capture of an encampment used by government-linked forces, threatened the roads connecting Taiz, Hodeida, Mokha and Bab al-Mandab. Once the encampment fell, Mokha lost much of its defensive depth. Withdrawal may have spared government units from encirclement, but it also handed the Houthis a major victory and a foothold farther down the coast. The map shows areas of control and the main front lines in western and eastern Yemen as of September 2026. Source: Crisis Group research / CRISIS GROUP The speed of the coastal front’s collapse reflected a deeper weakness in the anti-Houthi camp. An amalgam of government-aligned forces – the National Resistance, Giants Brigades, National Shield and Taiz axis units – were defending the coast but each with separate chains of command and sources of supply. They were not functioning as a single army with integrated reserves and air defence. These formations historically also had separate relationships with outside patrons. Saudi Arabia supports some of them, but the United Arab Emirates had stood up a number of others, and its withdrawal from Yemen in January, following a falling-out with the Yemeni government and Riyadh, left a political and logistical breach that complicated communications within the coalition. The Houthis exploited the gaps. Once its line began to break, the government had no unified command capable of coordinating retreats, reinforcements or counter-attacks. For the Houthis, the advance’s value lies in the momentum it generates for their domestic agenda, especially in tandem with Iran’s actions in the Strait of Hormuz. They are cash-strapped, but if economic gain had been their principal objective, eastern Yemen would have offered more obvious rewards, given that it comprises the country’s main oil fields. Bab al-Mandab offers something better: influence over a maritime chokepoint at a moment when another, the Strait of Hormuz, is under severe pressure. This influence is powerful leverage for both the Houthis in talks with the Saudi-led coalition arrayed against them and for Iran in its showdown with the U.S. In previous negotiations, the Houthis had sought several measures, such as oil revenue sharing and payment of salaries to civil servants in areas under Houthi control. In 2023, shortly before Hamas’s 7 October attacks derailed the deal, they had arrived at an understanding with the Saudi-led coalition that gave them some of what they wanted, for instance opening Sanaa airport to flights to and from five international destinations. Now, emboldened by their march down the coast, the rebels are demanding the items above, but also much more: an end to Saudi support for the Yemeni government, Saudi withdrawal from Yemen and war reparations. They see cross-border attacks and control of heights overlooking Bab al-Mandab – which allows them to impose what they describe as an embargo on Saudi-linked shipping – as the means of achieving these ends. As for Iran, by compounding the disruption of commerce in the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis’ approach serves the goal of driving up oil prices, thus augmenting international and domestic political pressure on the Trump administration as the U.S. midterm elections in November draw near. High Stakes for the Saudis For Saudi Arabia, the Houthi advance sharpens an increasingly dangerous two-strait problem, in which its ships face peril in both the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab. Riyadh had tried to prepare for this contingency by strengthening Yemeni government forces, building multilateral deterrence arrangements and keeping channels open with the Houthis and Iran. All three elements of this strategy are now under strain. The coastal front’s breakdown exposed the limits of military consolidation, while international backing remains, for now, focused on sharing intelligence and defending the kingdom itself rather than battling the Houthis. Emerging agreements with Pakistan and Türkiye may bolster Saudi surveillance and air capabilities, but they are unlikely to alter the balance inside Yemen. As for the U.S., President Donald Trump has made clear his reluctance to get involved, saying the Houthis reached out before their offensive to assure Washington they were not looking for another fight like that during the 2023-2025 Gaza war, when they last menaced Red Sea shipping in a systematic way. European and Arab powers will likely support Riyadh, though they also have their limits. Finally, Saudi diplomacy with Tehran and the Houthis has clearly not changed these actors’ calculations. For the kingdom, economic stakes are high and rising. The Houthis resumed fire at Saudi-linked vessels in the Red Sea just as they also attacked Saudi energy facilities and Iranian-backed Iraqi Shiite armed groups launched missiles that led to closure of Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline. On 11 September, after the above-ground pumping stations were hit, Saudi Arabia closed the largely underground pipeline. The conduit had been carrying 3-4.5 million barrels per day toward the Red Sea, helping offset the constriction of the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, Saudi crude transits through Bab al-Mandab fell from more than 3.5 million barrels per day in early July to near zero in August. Riyadh has been relying more heavily on Egypt, shipping oil by tanker to Ain Sokhna on the Red Sea, then through the Arab Petroleum pipeline 320km north west to the Mediterranean. There, it is reloaded onto tankers headed for Europe, as well as for Asia around the Cape of Good Hope. That lengthy route was already adding time and cost; in addition, too few tankers were available. Even with reports of larger Saudi shipments through Hormuz under U.S. protection, the flow of oil from Saudi Arabia will remain lesser than usual, vulnerable to attack and thus more expensive. The combination of Houthi control of Bab al-Mandab and attacks on energy infrastructure will inevitably have consequences for Saudi Arabia’s economy, regional trade and global energy markets. Riyadh may conclude that it needs a measure of military success to prevent Houthi gains from becoming entrenched and push the group back toward negotiations. It is likely to combine airstrikes on Houthi positions on the western coast with greater support for Yemeni government forces seeking to recover lost ground, while it looks for alternative ways of shipping out its oil. But Saudi Arabia has little appetite for a return to the large-scale operation that proved so costly after it first intervened to reinstate the Yemeni government in 2015. In the absence of active U.S. involvement, its preferred course will be to enlist willing and able regional and European countries in its efforts to defend Red Sea shipping and its territory. It may also seek their logistical support for its airstrikes in Yemen, while leaving the ground war largely to Yemeni forces and trying to revive its diplomacy with Tehran and the Houthis. That approach could contain the immediate threat, but should it fail, a widening campaign could draw Yemen deeper into the Middle East war, expanding it to both shores of the Red Sea and hardening Saudi Arabia’s position toward Iran. A Way Out The danger is that both sides draw the wrong lesson from the latest fighting. The Houthis may conclude that territorial gains and maritime pressure can extract major political concessions, leading them to dig in demanding not just salary payments and reparations but political recognition as a legitimate authority in Yemen. But it is virtually impossible for Saudi Arabia to agree to such steps, which it would see as tantamount to surrender, with all of the attendant political and strategic costs. Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government may, in turn, try to reverse their fortunes by enlisting more countries on behalf of their campaign and opening several fronts at once, hoping that the Houthis will relent, notwithstanding the rebels’ record of resiliency under duress. Either course could tip Yemen back toward full-scale war and worsen what is already a catastrophic humanitarian crisis in the country. The first objective should thus be to freeze the military contest in place. That would entail the Houthis halting their offensive in Yemen and stopping attacks on Saudi territory and shipping. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government would refrain from opening new fronts and pair measures designed to defend their positions with steps that offer the Houthis incentives for restraint. These would include allowing regular commercial flights from Sanaa to the five destinations agreed upon in 2023 and progress on economic arrangements such as payment of civil servants’ salaries. Oman is best placed to broker such a deal, while opening space for the parties to return to negotiations on broader political issues. But Iran, too, should realise that the slide toward broader war could jeopardise its remaining contacts with Saudi Arabia and further nudge other regional countries to align against it. Rather than encourage the Houthis along their current path, it should use its leverage to push for a halt to attacks on Saudi Arabia and an end to further territorial conquest in Yemen. Of course, given how closely the Yemen conflict is connected to the U.S.-Iran confrontation, any such de-escalation would be greatly facilitated by easing tensions between Tehran and Washington – and any sustainable de-escalation likely would require as much. Efforts to that end have failed so far, but events in Yemen should serve as a reminder of the urgency. European and regional states should double down on collective efforts to revive a version of the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding reached in June, focused on removing the double blockades on the Strait of Hormuz; issuing waivers for Iranian energy exports; and freezing both new U.S. sanctions and Iran’s nuclear program. For all, the aim should be to work in concert to prevent the confluence of the two fronts from provoking an even wider war that could embroil other regional and international actors in the Red Sea. resume: On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 09/18/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 18 September 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities. Bamako has been struggling to contain an insurgency linked to al-Qaeda, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which killed 50 Malian soldiers in its latest attack on an army base last week. JNIM has lately allied with northern separatists who have also been fighting the Malian army. Historically, Algiers has been an important mediator between Bamako and northern armed groups. The warming of Algeria-Mali relations raises hopes that it might again play such a role, though maybe a more limited one given the Malian authorities’ increasingly sovereignist mindset. It could nevertheless help mitigate the conflict that has torn at Mali since 2012. PHILIPPINES Regional parliamentary elections took place on Monday in the Bangsamoro, the swathe of the southern Philippines that won autonomy in 2019 as part of a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). At least five people were killed and twenty injured during the vote, though violence was less widespread than feared, with incidents concentrated in a few locations. No party secured an absolute majority, meaning that politicians will likely need to form a coalition. Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht says the incoming government, slated for inauguration by 30 October, will likely pair former MILF rebels with representatives of the region’s traditional political clans, unless the ex-insurgents, who have split into two factions, can reunite. The elections were a big step forward for the Bangsamoro peace process, with all eyes now on a crucial meeting between national government and MILF delegations to discuss gaps in fulfilling the 2014 accord’s terms. 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. The Trump administration, which has sanctioned the ICC for its investigation of Israeli actions in Gaza, called on more African nations to “reclaim their sovereignty” by following in Chad’s footsteps. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says some Chadians will welcome N’djamena’s move on these grounds. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Tensions between the TPLF and Addis Ababa have been rising for months, especially after it ousted an interim regional administration established under a 2022 peace deal and reinstalled its own chair as regional president in April. The two sides now accuse each other of soliciting help from one of the main belligerents in Sudan. Independent details of the clashes are scarce, says Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell, but clearly neither side wanted to escalate further at this time. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. Six assailants in the bed of a pickup truck fired assault rifles and threw pipe bombs, stealing the rangers’ weapons and body armour before fleeing. They also wounded six civilians, including three children, one seriously. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Let those who provide shelter and the countries that harbour them know this”. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. U.S. - IRAN The U.S. and Iran continued to trade blows this week, putting Washington’s Middle Eastern allies in the crosshairs of Iranian drone and missile launch teams while U.S. forces enforced a renewed naval blockade of Iran and conducted daily strikes on sites inside the country. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump pledged to “destroy one bridge or power plant” every time Tehran fires at a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz – a threat quickly met by warnings of retaliation in kind by the Islamic Republic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says both sides appear convinced that inflicting greater physical damage and economic pain plays to their strengths, even at the risk of significant escalation. For now, this dynamic is persisting despite efforts by mediators to dial down tensions. YEMEN The Houthi rebels declared a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia Monday, vowing to strike any Saudi-linked vessel passing from the Red Sea through Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting those waters to the Gulf of Oman. A de facto truce had held between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government from 2022 until last week, when Saudi warplanes bombed the Sanaa airport and the Houthis fired missiles at the kingdom in respo nse. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said an oil tanker caught fire after the Houthis struck it near the kingdom’s Red Sea port of Jizan. The foreign ministry in Riyadh said Saudi Arabia would take all necessary measures to defend itself, while U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. would inflict “major military punishment” upon both the Houthis and their ally Iran if they attack shipping again. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says the risk of open hostilities, both in the Red Sea and along front lines in Yemen, is rising dramatically. 17 July 2026 CUBA Cuba’s power grid collapsed Tuesday for the third time in less than ten days and the sixth time so far in 2026. The island’s severe energy shortages began in January when the U.S. imposed an oil blockade, triggering a humanitarian crisis. The blockade is part of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to bring about wholesale political and economic change in Cuba, as negotiations between the two countries stall. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the U.S. appears to be using civilian pain as a weapon in its effort to oust Cuba’s communist regime. Havana should pursue meaningful and much needed reforms, regardless of what the U.S. does. But in the meantime Washington should lift the blockade so as not to create a humanitarian crisis in the pursuit of its goals, and avoid any further escalation. IRAN One month on, the 17 June memorandum of understanding that was to halt hostilities between the U.S. and Iran looks moribund. U.S. forces have been conducting near-daily strikes in Iran throughout the past week and resumed their blockade of Iranian shipping, while Iran has been firing drones and missiles at U.S. bases around the Gulf and in Jordan. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says that both sides remain nominally open to diplomacy. But the latest exchanges underscore a mutual willingness to use military escalation and economic disruption in gambits to strengthen positions at the negotiating table. LEBANON An Israeli airstrike Thursday killed two people in southern Lebanon, despite negotiations in Rome to end the conflict between Israel and Hizbollah. The latter rejects the Israeli-Lebanese talks, arguing that Lebanon should instead rely on the group’s patron, Iran, to secure a genuine ceasefire and Israeli troop withdrawal as part of a broader deal with the U.S. This position notwithstanding, Hizbollah has largely halted its own military operations in recent weeks. While Israel has reduced the intensity of its attacks, it persists in conducting lethal strikes in the south, where it continues to occupy territory. Crisis Group expert David Wood says the continued Israeli assaults undermine the historic direct diplomacy that is happening between Israeli and Lebanese officials. Left unchecked, Israel’s attacks could sour relations between Tehran and Washington even further, making it even more difficult to reverse the escalatory cycle that has taken off in the Gulf. 10 July 2026 ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE UN Secretary-General António Guterres opened the Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva Monday by reiterating a call for a ban on what are called Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems, arguing that “some decisions must remain forever human – none more than taking a human life”. Crisis Group expert Issandr El Amrani says it is urgent to regulate the use of AI in warfare: AI-aided weapon systems are enabling rapid processing of targets with decreased human oversight, with potentially grave consequences for civilians, as seen during Israel’s war in Gaza and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. These “killer robots” need not be fully autonomous to render human oversight largely meaningless. More than 120 states, mostly from the Global South, have endorsed such a ban. But countries that have this technology, including the U.S., the UK and Russia, oppose it, contending that current provisions under international humanitarian law are sufficient. CHINA China test-fired a long-range ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine in the South Pacific Monday, its first such exercise in these waters in two years. Beijing characterised the missile test as part of routine annual training that comports with international law, stressing that it was not directed at another country. Australia, Japan and New Zealand raised objections, however, with Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong calling the test “destabilising” for the Asia Pacific and Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara describing it as “a grave concern” for the world. Crisis Group expert William Yang says the test sends a signal to the U.S. and allies that Beijing is determined to push back against what it views as attempts to contain China’s rise. The test took place on the same day that Australia signed a mutual defence agreement with Fiji. It will likely push other Asia Pacific countries both to deepen such cooperation and to accelerate their own military modernisation. SOUTH SUDAN On Sunday, opposition fighters killed James Kueth Makuach, commissioner of Akobo county in Jonglei state, in what President Salva Kiir’s government described as an “assassination”. Makuach had belonged to the party of former Vice President Riek Machar, who was arrested on sedition charges last year amid fighting between his loyalists and government forces. In April, Makuach defected to Kiir’s camp. The president then reappointed him as county commissioner, breaching South Sudan’s 2018 peace accord, which allotted this post to Machar’s group. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the Akobo attack, which also took the lives of two other government officials, is part of an escalation in clashes in Jonglei over the past week. But it appears to have been an act of political retribution rather than a push for territory or another military objective. Makuach’s killing underscores the dangers of proceeding with national elections planned for December with no political consensus in Juba and swathes of the country embroiled in civil strife. 3 July 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan flared again this week. On Sunday, Pakistani forces once again carried out strikes across the border in Afghanistan, saying they killed 29 militants. Islamabad said the strikes were retaliation for recent attacks inside Pakistan, including a Karachi assault that killed three security personnel. According to the UN, at least 28 civilians were killed and another 49 injured in the strikes. Pakistan accuses the Afghan Taliban of sheltering anti-Pakistan militants, which Taliban officials deny. On Wednesday, Afghanistan said it carried out strikes inside Pakistan, targeting ISIS and other armed opposition groups. Islamabad denies Taliban accusations of harbouring such groups and noted that it had intercepted four drones launched from Afghan territory. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says outside mediators should push the sides toward practical border and security arrangements before the cycle of strikes and counterstrikes escalates further. NIGERIA Violence is again escalating in north-western Nigeria. Long plagued by bandits who engage in mass kidnappings for ransom, pillage and extortion, the region is also now seeing increased jihadist activity. Together, bandit and jihadist attacks killed over 150 people in Katsina, Kebbi, Sokoto and Zamfara states in June, a notable uptick from previous months. On 28 May, Islamic State Sahel Province claimed what appears to be its first reported attacks in the region, in which eighteen soldiers and one police officer were killed in Kebbi and Sokoto states. Amid this escalation, on 20 June prominent bandit leader Bello Turji claimed responsibility for deadly attacks on troops and declared his group ready for either peace talks or prolonged war with the government. If the bandit and jihadist threats are not reined in, says Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi, north-western Nigeria could become part of the wider belt of instability in the Sahel. SUDAN Fighting centred on El Obeid, North Kordofan’s state capital, has intensified in recent weeks as drone strikes increase and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) mobilise around the city, raising fears of encirclement and blockade. UN relief chief Tom Fletcher warned Tuesday that El Obeid risks becoming “another El Fasher”, referring to North Darfur’s capital, which endured a prolonged siege before falling to the RSF last October and suffering mass atrocities. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says a siege of El Obeid would deepen the humanitarian crisis facing civilians, many of whom have already fled to the city from fighting elsewhere. Meanwhile, the increased use of drones against El Obeid could allow for sustained attacks through the now-beginning rainy season, when ground fighting has typically slowed. 26 June 2026 BOLIVIA President Rodrigo Paz declared a state of exception starting Saturday after more than 50 days of protests triggered by a land reform law and planned austerity measures. Authorities say at least 37 people have been injured in clashes between demonstrators and police. The decree bans the protesters’ roadblocks that have paralysed commercial traffic, causing shortages of basic goods in the administrative capital La Paz, and (temporarily) allows the armed forces to assist police in reopening key routes. It does not, however, suspend fundamental rights, as is often the case with states of exception in Latin America. Before making the declaration, Paz had signed an agreement to “pacify” the country with the biggest trade union, the Bolivian Workers’ Central, which withdrew from the streets. Most of the roadblocks have vanished since the measure took effect. But Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says tensions remain high. The unrest could erupt anew if the government fails to deliver on socio-economic commitments it made to the union or if other groups involved in the protests, including campesinos and Indigenous people, decide to resume the pressure. COLOMBIA Right-wing Abelardo de la Espriella won Sunday’s presidential runoff by the thinnest margin in Colombian history, defeating Iván Cepeda, who had campaigned on continuing leftist President Gustavo Petro’s social reform agenda. De la Espriella styles himself as an outsider. Boasting of his ties to U.S. President Donald Trump, who endorsed him before the vote, he has vowed to take an iron-fist approach to organised crime, for instance pledging to bomb narco-traffickers and build mega-prisons. Many Colombians are ready for such measures, says Crisis Group expert Renata Segura, having become frustrated with Petro’s attempts to negotiate “total peace” with criminal and other armed groups. But, as the close vote shows, nearly half the electorate is equally concerned about de la Espriella’s promise to circumvent checks and balances in pursuit of quick fixes. To protect public safety, Colombia needs to balance crimefighting with efforts to plug the gaps in state services that criminal organisations exploit, including for recruitment. The new government should not disregard negotiations, which, if done the right way, have proven an effective tool for reducing violence in Colombia. U.S. - IRAN U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed Wednesday that technical delegations from the U.S. and Iran will reconvene at the end of June to resume talks aimed at ending the conflict between the two countries. By the terms of the memorandum of understanding reached between the Trump administration and Tehran in Islamabad earlier this month, these working groups are tasked with negotiating the details leading to a “final deal”, including nuclear commitments by Iran and sanctions relief provisions by the U.S. Maintaining momentum in dialogue is critical, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, as the two sides have put forward clashing interpretations of the parameters they agreed to in Pakistan. The negotiations have many moving parts – related to the Strait of Hormuz and Lebanon, among other issues. In this ambitious scope lies promise, but also peril, as a setback on any one front could derail the whole endeavour. 19 June 2026 HAITI Visiting Tuesday, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said Haiti is suffering “the worst humanitarian crisis in the Western Hemisphere”. He toured the headquarters of the new Gang Suppression Force assembled to battle the criminal bands bedevilling the country. The UN released figures showing that gang violence has killed 2,300 people in the year to date and displaced a record 1.5 million more. Gangs have also kidnapped around 100 Haitians, including the defence ministry’s cabinet director last week. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says much hope rests on the new force, but whether it can deliver remains to be seen as it builds toward its mandated strength of 5,500. Gangs, meanwhile, appear to be adapting, attacking senior officials and expanding abductions into formerly safe areas, possibly to deter anti-gang operations where kidnapping victims are held. MYANMAR - CHINA Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted Myanmar’s coup-leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing on a state visit to Beijing this week. The two sides reaffirmed their “community with a shared future” and signed eighteen agreements covering areas including transport and development. The visit highlighted Beijing’s priorities in Myanmar: border stability, protection of Chinese investment, progress on select China-Myanmar Economic Corridor projects and continued cooperation in combating online scams and other transnational crime. Crisis Group expert Richard Horsey says the state visit’s symbolism may matter more than any individual deal, as it provides Min Aung Hlaing with a measure of the international legitimacy he craves. For China, meanwhile, it is an opportunity to lock in a dependency that provides growing strategic opportunities, while it pushes for greater calm in conflict-affected areas along the Myanmar border. UKRAINE - RUSSIA Overnight into Thursday, Ukraine launched its largest drone assault on Moscow since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, hitting an oil refinery and injuring at least seventeen people. Russia said it intercepted 194 drones around Moscow and nearly 1,000 drones and several cruise missiles nationwide over 24 hours. Ukraine said the attack was a response to Russian strikes earlier this week that damaged the UNESCO-listed Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra monastery. Moscow warned it would respond forcefully. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says the attacks highlight Ukraine’s efforts to demonstrate it can hit targets far inside Russia using deep-strike drones. But while such attacks create headlines, they have yet to affect the Kremlin’s warfighting ability and may harden support for the war among the Russian public. 12 June 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Pakistan launched air raids Wednesday across the border with Afghanistan, killing 26 Pakistani Taliban fighters, according to Pakistani Information Minister Attaullah Tarar. The Afghan authorities, however, said the strikes killed thirteen people, including eleven children. The air raids came one day after Pakistani Taliban fighters ambushed a security outpost in Pakistan’s north west, killing six officers. These incidents ended a month of calm in the conflict between the two countries. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says violent flare-ups like these are likely to persist as long as both countries’ security concerns remain unaddressed. IRAN - U.S. The fragile April ceasefire between Washington and Tehran wobbled as the two sides engaged in increasingly sharp exchanges of fire. U.S. forces launched repeated strikes on Iranian targets as Tehran retaliated by targeting U.S. bases in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait; Iran and Israel also traded blows for the first time in two months. On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened that the U.S. would take control of Kharg island, site of Iran’s main oil terminals, and other energy infrastructure. He backtracked later in the day, cancelling new strikes and insisting that a negotiated deal with Tehran was close. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says an agreement would be welcome if it steadies the shaky truce and gives Washington and Tehran a clear path to future negotiations. Those talks are likely to be fraught, however, and may not guarantee the end of hostilities if certain issues remain unresolved, such as Israel’s continued attacks on and occupation of over 20 per cent of Lebanon.
