But that ambition could be short-lived if Khamenei is targeted amid the hostilities or outmanoeuvred by other players in the regime's upper echelons. Many Iranians, meanwhile, are despairing at a leadership transition that so far promises more of the same. LEBANON Israel’s latest military escalation in Lebanon continued to wreak havoc this week. Since 2 March, when Hizbollah fired rockets toward Israeli territory for the first time in over a year, Israel has ramped up aerial bombardment, including of the capital Beirut, and forced hundreds of thousands to flee their homes. It has also sent more troops into southern Lebanon, with a view to establishing what it calls a “security zone” there. While Israel retains military superiority over Hizbollah, the Shiite party-cum-militia has put up a fight. On Wednesday, it launched a barrage of 100 rockets across the border, which triggered an especially brutal sequence of Israeli air raids. Crisis Group expert David Wood says neither of the belligerents appears ready to stop, even as Lebanese leaders scramble to find a diplomatic off-ramp. Already, the Lebanese public has paid a horrific price: the death toll has climbed to almost 700, and thousands more have seen their homes and communities destroyed. 6 March 2026 IRAN The U.S. and Israel launched massive airstrikes on Iran Saturday, hitting military installations and killing senior leaders, including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. In retaliation, Iran fired missiles and drones at Israel, as well as U.S. bases and commercial infrastructure in Gulf states. The conflict's reverberations have quickly spread from the Indian Ocean to the eastern Mediterranean. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Tehran looks prepared for a drawn-out confrontation, betting that it can steadily raise the psychological and economic costs to its adversaries, while maintaining cohesion at the top of the political system despite Khamenei’s demise. The U.S.-Israeli campaign appears open-ended, with no clear objective yet defined. Airstrikes can substantially degrade Iran's military capabilities but are unlikely to dislodge the regime, and even if they did, state collapse in Iran would risk unleashing far wider regional disorder. AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Border clashes continued this week after Pakistan declared “open war” with Afghanistan last Friday. The declaration followed Taliban retaliatory cross-border attacks after Pakistani airstrikes on purported Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) targets in Afghanistan on 21 February. Pakistan then carried out another series of strikes on 27 February, including in Kabul. Islamabad accuses Taliban authorities of sheltering the TTP, which has stepped up attacks in Pakistan. Kabul denies it. According to the UN, the latest fighting has killed dozens of civilians in Afghanistan and displaced tens of thousands, with reports also indicating civilian casualties in Pakistan. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says a drawn-out conflict serves neither side's interests. Outside actors should press Islamabad and Kabul to de-escalate. ECUADOR The U.S. Southern Command said Tuesday Ecuadorian and U.S. forces had begun operations to curb organised crime in Ecuador. They first went after the Colombian armed group Comandos de la Frontera, which is active along the Colombian border. Ecuador’s military says the operations will continue indefinitely. While details are classified, news reports indicate that the U.S. played an advisory role, without putting troops on the ground. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says such cooperation is not new, but the latest announcement signals deeper U.S. involvement. Security ties have deepened as President Daniel Noboa aligns with the Trump administration’s preference for using military force to combat drug trafficking. 27 February 2026 CHAD - SUDAN Chadian authorities Monday announced the immediate closure of the country’s border with Sudan. The decision followed what N’Djamena described as “repeated incursions” linked to Sudan’s war, after clashes around the Sudanese border town of Tina involving the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and militias aligned with Sudan’s army. Chad said the border would remain closed until further notice, while allowing humanitarian exemptions, including for refugees and returnees, as well as approved aid deliveries. Crisis Group expert Charles Bouëssel says N’Djamena should maintain vital cross-border aid and preserve trade that sustains displaced populations. It should also ensure that security and disarmament operations in the east are conducted with restraint and impartiality to contain intercommunal tensions and prevent Chad from being drawn further into Sudan’s war. CUBA Cuban authorities Wednesday accused ten people on a U.S.-registered speedboat carrying weapons and tactical gear of attempting infiltration of Cuban territory with “terrorist intentions”. Border guards shot four people dead and wounded six others aboard the boat after its occupants allegedly opened fire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. SYRIA ISIS released an audio statement last weekend denouncing Syria’s interim government and calling for a renewed campaign against its forces. The jihadist group has since claimed responsibility for several attacks on Syrian army personnel in the northern and north-eastern parts of the country. These developments follow last month’s reported mass escape from the al-Hol camp, which held over 20,000 detainees, many of them relatives of suspected ISIS fighters. Some of these people got away as security broke down during an offensive led by Damascus on the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis raises the risks associated with pregnancy, the report finds, though health services in conflict-affected places are generally already scarce. Some countries, such as Colombia and Ethiopia, have made progress in reducing maternal mortality through partnerships with NGOs with expertise in service provision in remote areas. But now aid cuts have put such programs in jeopardy, says Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing, even as women are dying in childbirth at alarming rates. Donor funds still available should be directed toward bolstering community-based health services, particularly in war zones, through such cost-effective means as midwifery. NIGERIA The Nigerian government announced Tuesday that the U.S. will dispatch 100 additional military personnel to assist in fighting jihadist groups in the northern part of the country. This deployment comes amid deadly attacks that killed 56 people in Niger state last weekend and 34 others in Kebbi state on Wednesday. These raids are part of a broader surge of violence that has claimed over 250 lives across north-central and north-western Nigeria in the past month. Hundreds more people have been abducted. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says jihadists and other armed groups are growing stronger in these regions and elsewhere, by exploiting gaps in rural and border security as government forces become increasingly overstretched. The U.S. aid notwithstanding, the government needs to urgently improve its response, including by expediting measures outlined under the “nationwide security emergency” President Bola Tinubu declared last November. U.S. - IRAN Iranian and U.S. delegations convened in Geneva Tuesday for talks about Tehran’s nuclear program, the second round of such negotiations this month. In parallel, the Islamic Republic’s foreign minister met with the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency for technical discussions. Both Iran and the U.S. noted a measure of progress, as did the Omani mediators, even as Washington continues to ramp up its deployment of military assets to the Middle East. But the gaps between the sides are still wide, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, even as regards what a possible agreement would cover. The negotiators have yet to wrestle with matters of substance. Tehran and Washington are aware of the high risks of failure, as well as the costs that fresh hostilities would bring. Yet the pace of diplomacy is lagging as momentum builds for confrontation. 13 February 2026 BANGLADESH The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a landslide victory Thursday in the country’s first national elections since the 2024 ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose Awami League was barred from contesting the vote. A concurrent referendum on the July Charter – a set of reforms negotiated by all the participating parties over the last year – passed by a wide margin. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. The incoming government will face daunting challenges, however, such as getting Bangladesh’s ailing economy back on track and improving security. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. More fighting could be in the offing if efforts to de-escalate tensions fail. WEST BANK Israel’s security cabinet Sunday approved measures that further cement Israeli control of the occupied West Bank, with the explicit goal of pre-empting the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. The move reflects an Israeli plan not only to annex all the Israeli settlements in the rural West Bank, but also to further limit what is left of nominal Palestinian autonomy and displace Palestinians from more built-up areas. Absent action that conditions trade and aid to Israel on policy changes, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein, international support for a two-state solution increasingly rings hollow. The annexation drive also undermines the Trump administration’s twenty-point plan for Gaza. 6 February 2026 GAZA Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip Wednesday, killing at least 24 Palestinians. The Israeli army claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander and responding to fire upon its troops, but civilians accounted for most of the casualties. The death toll among Palestinians in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire has now topped 550. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the latest violence underscores how tenuous the ceasefire remains despite formally entering its second phase, when the sides are supposed to begin addressing issues of long-term security, governance and reconstruction. Diplomats need to press Israel to release its chokehold on Gaza and push for continued progress on the truce’s terms. PAKISTAN Police backed by soldiers reportedly killed more than 200 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) fighters in raids throughout Balochistan, a south-western province next to Afghanistan, over the course of this week. The operations followed a rash of BLA attacks on police stations, military installations and residential areas that claimed 50 lives (33 civilians and 17 state personnel) over the weekend. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. But these events are bound to increase tensions between Islamabad and Kabul, which are already high following clashes between Pakistani and Afghan Taliban forces last October, and to further chill relations between Islamabad and New Delhi. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Amid these exchanges, Trump went so far as to suggest that Colombia, too, might be a target of U.S. military action. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting proved constructive, helping ease the tensions in the bilateral relationship and signalling that the two countries can continue working together to curb drug trafficking. The two presidents also discussed the tariff spat between Colombia and Ecuador, with Trump offering to mediate between these countries’ leaders. Resolving the immediate trade crisis could pave the way for stronger collaboration between Bogotá and Quito in fighting organised crime. 30 January 2026 COLOMBIA - ECUADOR The foreign ministers of Colombia and Ecuador met in Panama after a week in which a trade dispute escalated between the two countries. The standoff began last week, when Ecuador announced a 30 per cent tariff on Colombian imports, blaming Bogotá for insufficient action to stop drug trafficking along the shared border. Colombia retaliated with tariffs on Ecuadorian goods and a suspension of electricity exports. Ecuador then raised the fee for Colombian oil shipped through its pipelines tenfold from about $3 to $30 per barrel. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting indicates that the two capitals understand the dispute will hurt both economies as well as weaken both states’ ability to confront security challenges on the frontier. Rather than acting in isolation, the two should mount a coordinated cross-border response, which is likely to be more effective in fighting transnational criminal networks. IRAN U.S. President Donald Trump told Iran Wednesday that it risks "major destruction" if it fails to negotiate a nuclear deal with Washington. The ultimatum follows earlier warnings of U.S. intervention over the Islamic Republic's repression of protests. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Iran is unlikely to meet the White House's sweeping demands, which encompass nuclear, missile and regional concessions, raising the likelihood of confrontation at a time when the Islamic Republic already faces increasing diplomatic isolation, mounting economic problems and outrage at its brutal crackdown on dissent. SOUTH SUDAN The South Sudanese army announced Sunday it is launching a major offensive to recapture territory in Jonglei state that has been seized by opposition forces and allied militias since hostilities intensified in December. The UN warned this week that mass troop mobilisation and inflammatory rhetoric from senior commanders have significantly heightened the risk of violence against civilians. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the escalation signals a clear slide toward full-scale war. The rapidly expanding conflict threatens to draw in neighbouring states, including Uganda, and to deepen South Sudan’s dangerous entanglement in the war in Sudan. 23 January 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO M23 rebels withdrew from Uvira, near the Burundian border, over last weekend, ending a tense month in which they controlled the South Kivu town. They had promised to pull out, likely due to U.S. pressure following a December summit in Washington between their main outside backer, the Rwandan president, and his Congolese counterpart. The Congolese army and allied Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira this week, but in the interim chaos engulfed the town, with widespread looting and abuses against civilians, mainly by the Wazalendo. Of particular concern, says Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff, is the mounting ethnic tension in the area. The M23 insurgents, who portray themselves as defenders of the Tutsi people, took Uvira claiming that the Tutsi-related Banyamulenge living in town needed their protection. Primary responsibility for attacks on Banyamulenge residents lies with the Congolese authorities and their allies, but the rebels appear to have exposed these people to predictable retaliation after retreating. Another M23-aligned armed group, the Twiraneho, is involved in fighting around Uvira, also pointing to a pattern of inter-communal violence. GUATEMALA President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency Monday after inmates had taken more than 45 guards hostage at three prisons two days earlier. After the authorities regained control of one of the facilities, gang members outside jail killed ten policemen in retaliation. The state of emergency limits citizens' rights and gives state forces special powers such as making arrests without cause. It echoes the iron-fist approaches to public safety pursued by leaders in El Salvador and Ecuador. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Arévalo, who won the 2024 election touting a progressive reform agenda but has since lost popularity, listened to demands from Guatemalans for a decisive response to an uptick in violent crime. If the measure delivers immediate results, it could help the president’s political standing. UGANDA Tensions simmered this week after the 15 January elections, which saw President Yoweri Museveni win another term with 71.65 per cent of the vote. The leading opposition candidate, Robert Kyagulanyi of the National Unity Party (NUP), rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. He remains in hiding after dodging a police raid – staged for reasons that remain unclear – on his residence. The president's powerful son, army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said on social media Tuesday Kyagulanyi would be treated as an "outlaw/rebel" if he did not surrender within 48 hours. (He later deleted this and other inflammatory posts.) Meanwhile, authorities charged more than 100 NUP members with involvement in election day violence. An internet blackout has made details of the incidents difficult to verify. The official death toll is twelve, but both Kyagulanyi and Muhoozi have cited higher figures. The government says ten died when its forces were attacked at an opposition legislator's home, a version of events sharply contested by others who were present. Crisis Group expert Meron Elias says the opacity of events, along with Muhoozi’s threats, will likely keep the political temperature high following the polarising vote. 16 January 2026 CUBA The bodies of 32 Cuban soldiers killed during the 3 January U.S. raid in Venezuela arrived in Havana Thursday. Cuba is facing considerable uncertainty after U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday urged its government to “make a deal” or face the consequences, vowing that the U.S. would cut the Venezuelan oil supply to the island nation, which is heavily dependent on these deliveries for its energy needs. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Washington appears to be calculating that a deepening economic crisis in Cuba will mobilise the masses to bring about the regime’s collapse. The Cuban regime retains a strong military and solid ties to Russia and China, however, and previously has not hesitated to crush dissent. GREENLAND Several European NATO members have deployed troops to Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, to beef up infrastructure and carry out joint military exercises after U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly stated that the U.S. intends to acquire the island, by force if necessary. Wednesday’s meeting among the U.S., Greenland and Denmark in Washington failed to resolve “fundamental disagreement” on Greenland’s future, according to the Danish foreign minister. With Europe already buffeted by Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, says Crisis Group expert Olga Oliker, this crisis will have dire implications for the future of NATO and European security writ large if the U.S. does not back down. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. Two challengers – Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and Henri-Marie Dondra – have called for annulling the vote, alleging fraud, while the main opposition coalition boycotted the ballot, citing an uneven playing field. The disputed poll coincided with renewed violence in the south east. Fighters linked to the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) – a Zandé self-defence militia – disrupted voting in Bambouti. Clashes then spread, including AAKG attacks on government forces around Zémio in early January. The AAKG was initially aligned with Bangui but later broke with the government after its rapprochement with a Fulani-led armed group that the militia accuses of encroaching on Zandé land. Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji says the AAKG may be digging in to battle the state. Stability during Touadéra’s new term will hinge on promoting intercommunal dialogue in the south east, better integrating militias under army command, and reducing regional isolation through development and security reform. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. The army must soon move toward disarming Hizbollah north of the Litani, where the group refuses to comply – driving up the risk of internal discord. Yet Lebanese leaders also know that Israel will almost certainly respond to any hold-ups in disarming Hizbollah with severe military escalations, inflicting still more pain on their embattled country. titre: A Pivotal Moment in Uniting Post-Assad Syria
resume: A Pivotal Moment in Uniting Post-Assad Syria eschelhaas Thu, 09/17/2026 - 12:17 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Syrian President Ahmed Al-Shara, right, and Syrian Democratic Forces commander Mazloum Abdi, left, attend a session at the presidential palace in Damascus. Rami Alsayed / NurPhoto / via AFP Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 17 September 2026 15 minutes A Pivotal Moment in Uniting Post-Assad Syria The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, which long enjoyed de facto autonomy in north-eastern Syria, have dissolved. But tensions in the region remain high as talks about integration with the central state proceed. Further compromise would set a useful precedent for other parts of the country. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Syria The scene on 25 August, like countless others in Syria of late, would have been unimaginable a mere two years ago. Mazloum Abdi, commander-in-chief of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), the Kurdish-led group that had autonomously run much of the country’s north east for some fourteen years, stood in Damascus beside the flag of Syria’s former opposition and new state, announcing the SDF’s dissolution and taking on the role of adviser to President Ahmad al-Sharaa. Beyond marking Abdi’s transition to senior government official, the event represented a pivotal moment in the process aimed at integrating the SDF’s institutions into the Syrian state. Damascus and the SDF leadership have come a long way since their troops clashed in early 2026, but difficult questions lie ahead as they continue talks to define the next phase of integration. Deepening cooperation – and providing further clarity to address Syrian Kurds’ concerns about their security and role in governance – is the best way forward. Progress amid Frustration While it has made important progress, the SDF integration process has also been bumpy, generating its fair share of frustrations. Disappointment is particularly acute among the group’s core Kurdish constituency: the deal reached in late August is the latest in a series of compromises leaving the north east far less autonomy than it had enjoyed during most of Syria’s civil war. The shortfall is due partly to the dramatic shift in U.S. policy following the fall of former President Bashar al-Assad’s Baathist regime, as Washington embraced al-Sharaa’s government and wound down its decade-long partnership with the SDF. But the SDF’s own miscalculations also played a role. After agreeing with Damascus in March 2025 to define integration arrangements by year’s end, it dragged its feet. That strategy proved ill-advised. Government forces pressed their advantage on the battlefield in January, and the SDF saw its hand weaken. Tensions prompted by this confrontation linger to this day. Still, the integration process has proven successful in several key respects. It ended weeks of armed conflict that, just nine months ago, threatened to plunge northern Syria into further violence along ethnic lines; secured unprecedented Syrian government commitments to Kurdish rights; enabled the return of thousands of Kurdish families to their homes after years of displacement, partially reversing war-induced demographic changes; and improved prospects for separate talks in neighbouring Türkiye that aim to end decades of insurgency by the Kurdistan Workers Party or PKK, with which the SDF has deep ties. Scepticism of integration runs deep among Kurds, even as prominent Arab voices call for accelerating it. The SDF’s official dissolution marks the beginning of a new, critical phase. Important gaps between the sides remain, notably over the degree to which former SDF-aligned institutions can maintain coherence as they become part of state structures. The parties will also have to contend with countervailing popular pressures in the north east – scepticism of integration runs deep among Kurds, even as prominent Arab voices call for accelerating it. Unrest following the killing of a Kurdish soldier on 10 September has deepened the polarisation. If Damascus and the former SDF leadership can address these issues together, they could simultaneously consolidate the state’s writ and provide the former SDF with substantive roles in local and central governance. This outcome would do more than benefit both sides; it also could help clarify options for addressing similar challenges in other parts of a country still recovering from years of brutal civil war. A Series of Negotiations The ceremony on 25 August marked the latest in a series of understandings between the SDF and the central state. The first one, reached in March 2025, was very broadly framed and left many issues unresolved; months of deadlock in talks aimed at fleshing it out gave way to weeks of armed confrontation in early 2026. The subsequent 29 January agreement broke the impasse, reflecting the decisive shift in the balance of power after the government’s rapid military advance. This deal outlined a partial framework for integrating the troops, institutions and lands under SDF control into the Syrian state, but it did not answer key questions concerning the degree and pace of assimilation, among other practical details. Talks continued between the two sides to iron out these issues. At one level, they involved President al-Sharaa, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani, Mazloum Abdi and other senior north-eastern figures, who met occasionally to overcome key obstacles. Day-to-day discussions were left to a team appointed by al-Sharaa, working alongside former senior SDF officials named to government positions and other influential figures in the north east. U.S. diplomats, led by presidential envoy Tom Barrack, supported the process, but with a much lighter touch than during the direct mediation in which they engaged throughout much of 2025. Inevitably, these talks reflected the new balance of power that tilted heavily in the central state’s favour after the SDF’s military setback. The organisation nonetheless retained leverage, however diminished: as SDF leaders were well aware, Damascus was eager for them to officially dissolve the group and thus demonstrate their genuine commitment to integration. Weeks of intermittent exchanges centred on two issues in particular: the roles senior north-eastern figures would play in the central government and the scope of Kurdish-language instruction in schools. Kurdish representation at such senior levels of state power is a clear departure from the decades of exclusion and neglect the community endured under Baathist rule. The two sides finally reached a package of understandings on those matters in the hours preceding the SDF’s 25 August dissolution announcement. Mazloum Abdi agreed to become a presidential adviser, while Ilham Ahmad, head of the SDF’s external relations and a central player in the negotiations, assented to taking a seat in the Syrian parliament. These positions are of a lower rank than those informally suggested by SDF leaders, U.S. officials and other intermediaries, who had floated the idea of Abdi serving on Syria’s new national security council and Ahmad assuming a senior foreign ministry post. Nevertheless, they offer Kurdish leaders a foothold in the central government, supplementing key roles already filled by (former) SDF figures in the nascent integrated military and security structures in the north east. These include Sipan Hemo (until January, a leading SDF figure, now serving as assistant minister of defence for the north east) and Mahmoud Khalil Ali (aka “Siamand Afrin”), who previously led the SDF’s Asayesh security forces and is now deputy head of state security forces in the Hassaka governorate. Kurdish representation at such senior levels of state power is a clear departure from the decades of exclusion and neglect the community endured under Baathist rule. The two sides likewise reached a compromise on Kurdish-language education. Under the SDF-aligned administration, Kurdish had been the prevalent language of instruction in most classes offered in Kurdish areas. As the central government assumes responsibility for schools throughout the north east, SDF negotiators had aimed to maintain as much Kurdish-language instruction as possible. At first, Damascus wanted to limit Kurdish-language classes to just two hours per week. In the end, the central government agreed that schools in areas where Kurds form a significant percentage of the population would provide three hours weekly of Kurdish-language instruction and a fourth hour of “activities” in Kurdish. It also consented to having four core subjects – social studies, history, geography and philosophy – offered in Kurdish during the current academic year, albeit not necessarily beyond that. This compromise built on Damascus’s decision in June to recognise diplomas previously issued by the SDF-linked administration. It also expanded on points outlined in a decree issued by al-Sharaa in January – which, in addition to broader commitments on Kurdish rights, acknowledged Kurdish as a national language and permitted elective Kurdish-language courses. Though the August agreement went beyond Damascus’s previous positions, it still fell short of aspirations held by many Syrian Kurds. In subsequent days, Kurdish organisations (including some allied with the SDF) demonstrated in favour of expanded Kurdish instruction. In a nod to those demands, Mazloum Abdi noted in his remarks announcing the SDF’s dissolution that “we will work to implement this decision [on education] in the current year, so that we can build on it in the future”. Gaps Ahead Meanwhile, other files remain subject to further negotiation. The two sides have yet to fully agree on how members of the SDF’s Women’s Protection Units (in Kurdish, Yekîneyên Parastina Jinê , or YPJ) will be incorporated into government forces. Damascus rebuffed SDF proposals to integrate the all-women force into Syria’s nascent post-Assad military, which currently excludes women from combat units. It suggested instead that they be placed under the interior ministry, which in recent months has begun recruiting women throughout the country into police forces. SDF and YPJ leaders have signalled openness to this idea in principle, while pushing to maintain the YPJ’s structural coherence and focus on counter-terrorism , building on its role in combating ISIS. Damascus and Kurdish leaders continued discussing this matter amid their late August meetings, but they have yet to reach an understanding. Beyond these immediate practical gaps lies a more essential divergence that has marked negotiations since early 2025, namely over how centralised each side believes the new Syrian state should be, and thus over how to define integration , particularly in Kurdish population centres. Both concur that the north east should be fully incorporated within state institutions, but they differ on the degree to which former SDF-linked structures, military as well as civilian, should be able to retain their coherence and the extent to which authority would be locally delegated. To date, Damascus has been prepared to live with a light-touch integration of Kurdish entities into the all-important military and security sectors. To date, Damascus has been prepared to live with a light-touch integration of Kurdish entities into the all-important military and security sectors, with SDF and Asayesh forces maintaining much of their structural integrity under the command of senior officers appointed by Damascus. As a result, Kurdish residents’ primary day-to-day interaction with government forces in the north east has been with Kurdish personnel reporting to an integrated chain of command. Such was still the case after the central state sent more of its forces to the region, most recently through the 1 September deployment of additional personnel to Hassaka city. The approach appears to have been largely successful, extending the reach of state sovereignty throughout the north east while keeping public safety in local hands and mitigating concerns among Kurds about how they would fare with non-Kurdish forces. But the written agreements the sides have signed thus far do not clearly define the terms of these arrangements. Nor do they indicate how long the arrangements will stay in place, leaving open the question of whether and to what extent Damascus might push to deepen central authority as time goes by. This ambiguity was a key reason why the SDF repeatedly advocated for solidifying the understandings through some form of constitutional guarantee. Damascus demurred, deferring talks about that demand to forthcoming discussions of Syria’s future constitution. Kurdish leaders have also made clear their intention to press in those discussions for more explicit constitutional linguistic and cultural protections. The timeframe and process for drafting the constitution remain uncertain, as does the mechanism that would allow for input by Kurdish leaders. Addressing Challenges, Clarifying Gains Beyond these gaps, three challenges stand out: returning displaced persons to their homes; managing incidents that threaten to ignite ethnic and political tensions; and addressing the sharp cost-of-living increase that is, at least in part, a by-product of integration. The issue of displaced persons counts among the most sensitive in northern Syria. Both Kurds and Arabs suffered large-scale displacement during the civil war, with tens of thousands of Kurds forced to leave their homes during offensives in which Syrian opposition forces backed by Türkiye seized the district of Afrin (in north-western Syria) and the towns of Ras al-Ayn and Tel Abyadh (in the north east) from Kurdish-led forces allied with the SDF. Thousands of Arab residents also fled during various SDF advances. Some of the resulting demographic changes persist to this day, exacerbating ethnic tensions that for decades were stoked by the forced Arabisation policies of Bashar al-Assad and his father, Hafez. Both Damascus and Kurdish leaders assert that securing the safe return of displaced persons is a priority. Both Damascus and Kurdish leaders assert that securing the safe return of displaced persons is a priority, and they have restated their commitment to that goal at every stage of negotiations. Together, they have achieved significant progress since the 29 January agreement. Between March and July, some 11,000 families returned to Afrin in convoys organised by government officials (including Damascus appointees and former SDF figures) in coordination with a committee representing the displaced. The influx of returnees has helped both restore Afrin’s social fabric and mitigate concerns among senior Kurdish figures who harboured doubts about integration. The government launched a similar cooperative effort to facilitate returns to and around Ras al-Ayn, an ethnically mixed town known in Kurdish as Serê Kaniyê. Yet serious obstacles have emerged of late. On 10 August, armed men attacked the first convoy carrying Kurdish families returning to Ras al-Ayn. As reports of violence spread, demonstrations erupted in Kurdish population centres in the north east, with a number of protesters reportedly attempting to break into central government facilities. Competing narratives of what motivated the attacks are difficult to parse, and no settled account has emerged. Kurdish leaders and government officials worked together to restore calm, with Mazloum Abdi calling for demonstrators to preserve state institutions and government forces announcing the arrest of several Ras al-Ayn assailants. The incident nevertheless underscored the limits of state authority in an area that until 2025 was controlled by poorly disciplined rebel factions, which seized it from the SDF during a Turkish-backed offensive in 2019. Those factions have since been incorporated into state forces, but their assimilation is far from complete. The government suspended returns to Ras al-Ayn town until conditions improve, which will entail addressing property disputes and dampening ethnic tensions in a location awash with guns. Their success in developing a cooperative model notwithstanding, the government and Kurdish leaders face significant challenges in trying to build on the example of Afrin. The returns file is but one example of how local sparks can ignite broader tensions in the north east. On 10 September, Sipan Hazni, a Kurdish former SDF soldier who had recently joined an integrated Syrian army unit, was kidnapped and brutally killed. Purported images of the murder circulated online, along with reports alleging that the killers were Arab tribesmen. As in August, protesters poured into the streets in Kurdish-majority towns and neighbourhoods, and some reportedly attempted to storm government facilities. This time, however, events escalated further in the town of Kobani (known in Arabic as Ayn al-Arab). The interior ministry deployed additional forces to the town, citing altercations that had left security personnel with injuries. Those forces arrested several demonstrators, then attempted to transport some of them from a prison in Kobani to Aleppo – in other words, from a facility still administered by former SDF-aligned personnel to one run by the central government. A prisoner reportedly lit a fire to protest the transfer, and nine detainees perished in the flames. Reactions in each camp underlined the challenges integration faces, but also its potential. Mistrust was evident, particularly in the episode’s early hours. An interior ministry official said some of those arrested were former SDF fighters, implying that elements of the former SDF that oppose integration were fanning unrest. Within SDF circles, the government’s deployment of reinforcements and attempt to transfer Kurdish detainees to facilities outside the north east bolstered concerns about further centralisation of security authority. Yet despite such misgivings, officials from both camps cooperated to quell the disturbance and signalled they would work together to investigate the incidents culminating in the prison fire. Mazloum Abdi’s role was particularly salient: meeting in Kobani with grieving family members and a range of local notables, he addressed concerns about the unrest and the integration process in his new capacity as adviser to President al-Sharaa. The combination of subsidy cuts and surging energy prices has hit the north east hard, with knock-on effects throughout the local economy. Meanwhile, economic conditions in the north east pose another political challenge, as the cost of living in areas previously governed by the SDF-linked administration has risen significantly. Though inflation is occurring throughout Syria, the surge in prices in the north east during recent months has been particularly acute. It has been driven, at least in part, by changes resulting from integration. When the former SDF-linked administration controlled the area’s oil extraction and economic policy, it provided cheap fuel and various subsidies to electricity generators, bakeries and other facilities, as well as to the vital agricultural sector. But as Damascus extended its writ, it scaled back these benefits, in keeping with its overall determination to maintain fiscal discipline. The combination of subsidy cuts and surging energy prices has hit the north east hard, with knock-on effects throughout the local economy. A steep hike in fuel prices announced by the government on 13 September exacerbated this dynamic, sparking protests in and beyond the north east. Insofar as north-eastern residents link the ensuing financial pain to integration, their faith in the process is fading. As fears resulting from the January military confrontation subside, Kurds in particular are liable to assess integration in terms of its practical impact. They have much to welcome: Kurds now enjoy legal recognition and state institutional roles that were hard to imagine under the previous regime, and the shift from SDF to state governance has eased some of their hardships, including difficulties with their educational diplomas, which previously were not recognised anywhere outside the north east. But, for now at least, the increased cost of living is undermining support among many who otherwise see integration’s benefits and sharpening grievances among those who oppose it. Eyes on the Prize The progress of integration to date is a testament to the foresight of the two sides’ respective leaders. But they need to remain focused on the significant challenges that lie ahead. The stakes are high and the payoff for further progress potentially great. Whereas any setback could have dangerous ramifications for the area’s stability, success could highlight constructive options for addressing governance and integration elsewhere – particularly in southern Syria, where the Druze-majority governorate of Suweida remains outside government control. While the local and geopolitical circumstances differ, the factors that will likely make or break integration in the north east would also be critical to an integration process in Suweida: incorporating local forces to lead in providing day-to-day security; ensuring that the area is well-represented in central government structures; and delivering clear economic gains and better services to the population. Having accomplished several of its priorities – notably extending the state’s institutions and command throughout the north east – Damascus ought to now focus on demonstrating the concrete benefits of integration. The more it is seen to improve security, governance and quality of life for Syrians in the north east, the more credibility integration will attain, including among those who remain understandably apprehensive of central state power after decades of suffering under the Assads. To that end, Damascus should clarify that the SDF’s former Asayesh personnel will form the long-term core of local security forces. It should also ensure that leaders such as Mazloum Abdi and Ilham Ahmad can play substantive, visible policymaking roles, including in drafting a new constitution – progress on which remains essential to Syria’s broader post-Assad transition. Mitigating economic pain in the north east will prove challenging in light of Syria’s fiscal constraints, but Damascus could discuss prospects for external aid to support integration with the U.S., as well as with European and Gulf Arab states. With the SDF now dissolved and several of its leading figures serving as senior government officials, integration may play out less as a negotiation between two parties and more as a mix of bargaining and collaboration among elements of the state. This shift arguably is already well under way locally, as illustrated by how the two camps have worked together to ease displaced persons’ return and to restore calm when tensions have boiled over. If Damascus aims to turn the north east’s integration into a model, building on that cooperation – including at the national level – would be an important way to strengthen its appeal. titre: The Houthis’ Advance to Bab al-Mandab: Has Yemen’s War Returned?
resume: The Houthis’ Advance to Bab al-Mandab: Has Yemen’s War Returned? eschelhaas Wed, 09/16/2026 - 17:32 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List The Houthis’ Advance to Bab al-Mandab: Has Yemen’s War Returned? Online Event Tuesday, 22 September 2026 10am Washington, DC | 4pm Brussels | 5pm Sanaa Please register here if you would like to attend this online event. Over the past week, the Houthis have swept down Yemen’s western coast and reached Bab al-Mandab, unravelling a defensive line that had held for years, and exposing just how fragmented the government camp’s forces had become. A string of retreats was decisive, as the National Resistance, Giants Brigades and other nominally allied units, each with its own command and backers, lost Khokha, Mokha and the roads linking Taiz, Hodeida and the coast, fighting side by side but never as one army. A foothold near one of the world’s busiest shipping chokepoints gives the Houthis fresh leverage over Saudi Arabia, just as Riyadh’s containment strategy is under strain. It also ties their campaign more closely to Iran’s entrenched standoff with Washington: any disruption to shipping through Bab al-Mandab would compound the effects of restrictions around the Strait of Hormuz, raising the economic costs of a wider confrontation. In this online event, Crisis Group brings together leading experts to discuss how the front collapsed so quickly, what the new balance of power means for Taiz, Marib and the other fronts still in play, and whether Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government and Yemen’s neighbours can keep this round of fighting from sliding into a wider war. Panellists: April Longley Alley | Senior Fellow, The Washington Institute Ahmed Nagi | Senior Analyst, Yemen, Crisis Group Peter Salisbury | Adjunct Professor, Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs Moderator: Yasmine Farouk | Project Director, Gulf and Arabian Peninsula, Crisis Group The panel discussion will be held in English and will be live-streamed on YouTube . 0 0

titre: Ten Challenges for the UN in 2026-2027
resume: Ten Challenges for the UN in 2026-2027 eschelhaas Mon, 09/14/2026 - 10:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Candidates for United Nations Secretary-General position participate in a debate at the UN General Assembly Hall in New York, on July 23, 2026. Leonardo MUNOZ / AFP Special Briefing 15 / Multilateral Diplomacy 14 September 2026 20+ minutes Ten Challenges for the UN in 2026-2027 As the 2026 General Assembly begins, the UN remains hobbled by cost cutting and big-power wrangling. The new Secretary-General to be chosen soon cannot cure all that ails the organisation, but much can be done to put its still considerable capacity to work. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Download PDF Full Report (en) Related Tags Global What’s new? Leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly will find an organisation in need of revival. UN diplomacy aimed at halting wars and easing civilian suffering remains paralysed, while funding cuts have weakened UN capacity. States have one eye to the future as they prepare to appoint a new Secretary-General. Why does it matter? The UN remains the only universal forum for global cooperation on war and peace, even as the international order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope the next Secretary-General can help the organisation dispel its malaise and forge a new direction. What should be done? A new Secretary-General cannot resolve the world’s crises overnight, but this person should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capabilities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. I. Overview When world leaders last met at the UN General Assembly in September 2025, the organisation was in disarray, reeling from U.S. aid freezes and major-power disputes. A year on, the organisation remains trapped in an open-ended crisis, even after an additional round of cost cutting and other reforms. Under the Trump administration, the U.S. has morphed from a flawed champion of the international legal order into an overt scofflaw. While the U.S. has not repudiated the multilateral system anchored by the UN, it has done great damage to the organisation, insisting on shrinking multilateral peace operations, slow-rolling funding and tried to impose its ideological agenda. The Security Council continues to be a forum for hashing out big-power differences – with the U.S., Russia and China coming to agreement on second-tier files. But as regards the most salient peace and security challenges today – the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, as well as Ukraine and Sudan – the UN is notable mainly for being stuck. The next Secretary-General cannot cure all that ails the UN, but creative diplomacy could be useful in putting its still considerable capacity to work. If the overall mood at the UN is one of drifting toward perdition, it is partly because everyone is waiting for change at the top of the system. Secretary-General António Guterres will complete his term at the end of December. A small batch of candidates – eight, at the time of writing – have been publicly and privately lobbying throughout the year to replace him. Most have been cautious in their campaigning, to avoid offending the major powers that dominate the selection process. UN insiders are watching with mixed feelings. Some hope that the next Secretary-General can bring new energy to the organisation and, assuming Washington is amenable, restore a measure of political relevance and financial stability. Others worry that the U.S., China and Russia will connive to choose a weak candidate firmly under their control and that the Trump administration will force the next UN chief to make even more radical cuts throughout the institution. The selection process has at least focused minds on what the UN, multilateral cooperation and international law exist to achieve. Many member states have emphasised that they would like to see the incoming Secretary-General do more to promote conflict prevention and resolution, which Guterres has sometimes given short shrift while pursuing other goals, such as international cooperation on artificial intelligence. Guterres no doubt felt that he had little to gain by focusing on geopolitical crises given the lack of consensus among the big powers. But there is now a widespread sense that the UN cannot pretend to be a useful platform for discussions of far-reaching issues like AI if governments do not believe that it can deliver on its core, UN Charter-defined purpose of maintaining peace and security. The crises of the last twelve months have also offered reminders of the extent to which the UN still offers a necessary if imperfect scaffolding for international cooperation. The Trump administration has grudgingly turned to the Security Council to endorse its conflict management efforts in Haiti and Gaza. Faced with the fallout of the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, such as closure of the Strait of Hormuz, governments around the world have stressed the importance of international legal principles including the prohibition of aggressive war, rules protecting civilians and civilian objects in conflict, and freedom of navigation. Though the UN has had a vanishingly small voice in diplomacy aimed at ending the Middle East war, both U.S. and Iranian officials have acknowledged that the Security Council should play some role – if only a ministerial one – in any peace deal. The UN ... remains best positioned to deliver humanitarian aid, mount peace operations and manage protracted crises that few other actors ... can handle. These are small consolations, but at a moment in which the U.S. and Russia are learning the limits of hard power in the Middle East and Ukraine, there is still space to reiterate the case for diplomacy, cooperation and respect for law. The next UN Secretary-General can make it. While it is foolish to expect a single administrator, however senior, to save the world, many small and midsize UN member states, as well as many major-power officials, are ready to heed a call to reinforce the lapsing international legal order. The UN also remains best positioned to deliver humanitarian aid, mount peace operations and manage protracted crises that few other actors – including the flailing U.S.-backed Board of Peace – can handle. It is possible that new leadership at the UN can give the organisation as a whole, and its peace and security pillar in particular, a new strategic direction. But amid deadly violence, regional rifts and institutional headaches, it is a near certainty that UN crisis management will continue to involve a great deal of firefighting and muddling through. This briefing, based on Crisis Group’s research at the UN and in the countries concerned, offers a guide to some of the most urgent issues. II. The Year in Review: Trends in UN Diplomacy The UN spent much of the past year adapting to a more assertive and transactional U.S. administration. Alongside long-running crises in Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan, the latest U.S.-Israeli war with Iran placed additional strain on Council diplomacy and the UN-backed international order. 1 Crisis Group Special Briefing N°14, Causes of Peace in an Era of Hard Power , 8 July 2026. Meanwhile, the UN’s multi-year liquidity crisis worsened, compounded by the U.S. aid cuts, disrupting operations at headquarters in New York and in the field. Steep reductions in voluntary contributions to UN humanitarian agencies forced the organisation to make difficult choices with its assistance, leaving many civilians affected by armed conflict with little support. Debates over the UN’s future simmered as member states began their search for the next Secretary-General. A year after Donald Trump’s return to the White House, the organisation was no longer in shock but adjusting to a new normal. A. Crisis Management and UN Diplomacy 1. The Security Council A year ago, Crisis Group observed that U.S. diplomacy at the Security Council under the newly installed Trump administration had lacked a clear direction. 2 Crisis Group Special Briefing N°13, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2025-2026 , 9 September 2025. The arrival of U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz in New York on the eve of the 2025 UN General Assembly marked the beginning of a more purposeful, and often determined, U.S. approach in the Council. Together with Panama, the U.S. secured Council authorisation for a new Gang Suppression Force for Haiti shortly after Waltz’s arrival, along with a UN logistics office to defray some of the Force’s costs (see Section III.4). 3 “ Haiti: Vote on a Draft Resolution Authorizing a ‘Gang Suppression Force’ and a UN Support Office* ”, Security Council Report, 30 September 2025; Daniel Forti, “ New Force to Battle Haiti’s Gangs Gets Security Council Blessing ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 1 October 2025; Crisis Group Latin America & Caribbean Report N°110, Undoing Haiti’s Deadly Gang Alliance , 15 December 2025. Less than two months later, the Trump administration – backed by its regional partners and Palestine – persuaded the Council to endorse its ceasefire plan for Gaza and establish the vaguely defined Board of Peace. 4 “Resolution 2803”, UNSC S/RES/2803, 17 November 2025; Daniel Forti, Richard Gowan and Max Rodenbeck, “ What to Look for as the Gaza Peace Plan Comes to the UN Security Council ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 November 2025. In both cases, the Council agreed to arrangements that concentrated decision-making authority in Washington and minimised the UN’s political and operational roles. With UN diplomacy on the war in Gaza lowered to a simmer (see Section III.3), the U.S.-Iran conflict became the Council’s defining crisis of the past year. Major-power tensions over Iran were already high at the UN prior to the outbreak of hostilities at the end of February. After the breakdown of nuclear diplomacy between the U.S. and Iran in 2025 and the twelve-day campaign launched by Israel (and joined by the U.S.) against Iran in June, France, Germany and the UK – three of the participants in the 2015 nuclear deal, or Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action – decided to reimpose “snapback” sanctions on Tehran that were otherwise set to expire that October. 5 Naysan Rafati and Daniel Forti, “ Iran Sanctions Snapback at the UN ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 25 August 2026. Beijing and Moscow rejected the legality of the reimposed UN sanctions, and in protest, they have obstructed business in all of the Council’s sanctions committees and thematic working groups since 2026 began. 6 China and Russia have blocked the appointment of the chairs and vice chairs of all subsidiary bodies, which require Council unanimity according to the body’s informal working methods. The chairs and vice chairs are responsible for leading each body’s meetings, briefing the Council on behalf of each body and managing its workflow. For more, see “ In Hindsight: A Second Year of Delays in the Allocation of Subsidiary Body Chairs ”, Security Council Report, 1 July 2026; Letter from the Security Council’s ten elected members , UNSC S/2026/636, 30 July 2026. Tensions in the Council gradually escalated after the U.S. and Israel once again attacked Iran on 28 February. Tensions in the Council gradually escalated after the U.S. and Israel once again attacked Iran on 28 February. China and Russia sharply criticised the two states during the Council’s first emergency meeting on the war. But even so they allowed passage of a Bahrain-led resolution condemning Iran’s retaliatory fire at its Gulf Arab neighbours days later, abstaining instead of vetoing it. Their posture suggested that preserving relations with the Gulf states was a higher priority than blocking a one-sided resolution that had no teeth. 7 Beijing and Moscow abstained from the vote. Russia also submitted a separate counter-resolution discussing the war’s root causes that got too few votes to be adopted. See “ Resolution 2817 ”, UNSC S/RES/2817, 11 March 2026. Their stances gradually hardened, however, as Washington pressed the Security Council to consider more coercive measures against Tehran. In early April, the Gulf states and the U.S. tabled a resolution for the Council to endorse a vaguely defined multinational naval coalition that would be tasked with reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Moscow and Beijing vetoed the text despite intense lobbying by Gulf capitals, arguing that the resolution would have given the U.S. open-ended authorisation to escalate its campaign. 8 The vote took place hours after U.S. President Donald Trump shared a social media message threatening to annihilate Iran. During its explanation of vote, Russia invoked the Security Council’s 2011 open-ended authorisation of NATO-led military action in Libya as a comparison to the proposed Gulf-U.S. initiative. Crisis Group interviews, UN diplomats, April-May 2026. See also remarks by the Russian Federation, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10130th meeting of the United Nations Security Council”, UNSC S/PV.10130, 7 April 2026. Weeks later, the U.S. and Gulf states drafted another resolution to demand that Iran open and demine the strait, while threatening sanctions for non-compliance. Despite finding over 138 co-sponsors, the U.S. and Bahrain did not submit the text for a vote, as they could not secure the support of Russia and China. Council diplomacy on the file has since stalled. Complex and sometimes volatile relations among the U.S., China, and Russia continue to shape the boundaries of Council diplomacy beyond the Gulf. After the reversal of U.S. Ukraine policy in early 2025, when the Trump administration stopped sending arms to Kyiv to resist Russia’s all-out invasion, Moscow may have expected Washington to press the Ukrainian government to make concessions in negotiations to end the fighting. Instead, U.S. statements in the Security Council have criticised Russia’s full-scale invasion and called on the Kremlin to agree to an immediate ceasefire. 9 Remarks by the United States, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10166th Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10166, 8 June 2026. More often than not, U.S. and Russian diplomats have sparred over UN responses to crises in the Middle East and Africa. By contrast, Washington and Beijing have shown willingness to strike occasional deals in the Security Council. Though they frequently clash, recent Council action has depended on a degree of cooperation between these geopolitical rivals. In September 2025, the U.S. agreed to pay nearly $680 million to the UN peacekeeping budget and drop its objections to China becoming penholder on the Council’s Afghanistan file in exchange for Beijing’s support for the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti. 10 Daniel Forti and Richard Gowan, “ Reading the Signals of China’s U.N. Security Council Role in the Afghanistan Mission Renewal ”, Just Security , 31 July 2026. U.S. diplomats also convinced their Chinese counterparts to support the delisting of Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa and Interior Minister Anas Khattab from the UN counter-terrorism sanctions list despite Beijing’s reservations. 11 Maya Ungar, “ UN Lifts Sanctions on Syria’s President as White House Visit Beckons ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 7 November 2025. Recalibrating UN operations in Myanmar Myanmar’s installation of a nominally civilian administration in April, following elections stage-managed by the military four months earlier, has created a dilemma for the UN. The elections have not restored state authority or legitimacy, and Naypyitaw does not have a credible strategy for ending the country’s armed conflict, either through negotiation or military victory. 130 Crisis Group Asia Briefing N°188, Myanmar’s New Administration: Military Consolidation, Not Transition , 3 June 2026. Humanitarian conditions continue to deteriorate as fighting, economic decline and fear of conscription grip the country. 131 “ Myanmar Humanitarian Update no. 51 ”, UN OCHA, 9 March 2026. Even so, more of Myanmar’s regional neighbours are giving the new administration de facto recognition, with Min Aung Hlaing – the coup leader who is now president – recently visiting India, China, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam. Beijing maintains a firm position limiting discussion of Myanmar at the UN, while Secretary-General Guterres has shown little willingness to invest political capital in the issue. Absent new diplomatic momentum in the near term, UN officials will need to calibrate engagement carefully to reduce harm, sustain livelihoods and support development without conferring legitimacy on abusive forms of rule. Much of this work will fall to the new UN leadership in Yangon. In October 2025, Guterres appointed veteran official Gwyn Lewis as resident and humanitarian coordinator ad interim, ending the ineffective practice of rotating the position among agency heads. 132 Lewis has the ad interim designation because the Secretary-General does not want to acknowledge the authorities politically by writing to seek their agreement to the appointment. See Crisis Group Special Briefing N°12, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2024-2025 , 10 September 2024. The resident coordinator will need to shape the UN’s engagement with the new administration while ensuring the organisation can continue delivering essential humanitarian and development assistance. Just as importantly, the office should provide clear strategic direction to the whole UN country team so that agencies operate according to a consistent approach within current political constraints. UN officials will also need to manage relations with Myanmar’s ethnic armed groups. Aid agencies already deliver assistance in parts of the country outside state control, working through local partners despite the absence of formal agreements with Naypyitaw. As the devastating March 2025 earthquake showed, the UN remains one of the few organisations capable of delivering international aid at scale to civilians in much of the country, including areas outside government control. 133 Richard Horsey, “ Support Vital for Myanmar’s Quake Victims, Despite Military Obstacles ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 1 April 2025; “ End of Mission Report United Nations Disaster Assessment & Coordination – Earthquake 7.7M Response – Myanmar (29Mar-16Apr 2025) ”, UN OCHA, 23 February 2026; “ First person: Myanmar aid workers brave conflict and harsh conditions to bring aid to earthquake victims ”, UN, 30 April 2025. Their support is therefore delivered off-budget – outside state systems – and depends on UN agencies for fiduciary oversight and distribution. Protecting the UN’s gender work in conflict settings The UN’s reform agenda has raised thorny issues about how the institution should organise its work to support women and girls. In late 2025, Secretary-General Guterres proposed merging the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) with UN Women as part of the UN80 initiative. 140 Other proposed mergers under UN80 include combining the UN Development Programme and the UN Office for Project Services; the UN Institute for Training and Research and the UN System Staff College; and the World Health Organisation and the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS. UNFPA leads the UN’s work on sexual and reproductive health, while UN Women (approximately one third the size of UNFPA) advocates for normative shifts on gender issues, including the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda, and distributes funding to NGOs for related programming. 141 With an annual budget of $1.53 billion, UNFPA’s model focuses on service delivery through 3,569 staff in 150 countries. “ As-Is Analysis: A Baseline for the UNFPA - UN Women Strategic Merger Assessment ”, UN80 Initiative, Work Package 4, Working Document, 6 March 2026. Whether the merger will come to pass is not clear. Amid aid cuts and pushback against gender equality worldwide, many member states and UN officials worry that combining these entities would hobble the UN’s work on gender, including efforts to support women and girls affected by conflict, for years to come. For more, see “ Independent Review of the UN System’s Capacity to Deliver on Gender Equality ”, Dalberg, 11 February 2023. The merger it proposed would bring together UNFPA and UN Women in a new entity with a unified voice. Recasting discussions of the future of UN peace operations Diplomats routinely cite peace operations as one of the UN’s flagship contributions to peace and security. But the Security Council has not authorised a large-scale blue helmet force for over a decade, and the number of troops and police personnel serving under the organisation’s banner has halved in the same period. There have also been few new UN Special Political Missions (SPMs), which are solely or largely civilian in nature. As noted in the introduction, the Trump administration has pushed for budget cuts to UN missions of all kinds, questioning their expense, efficiency and apparent lack of concrete goals. To guide discussions about how to revitalise this atrophying tool, the Secretary-General published a review of all forms of peace operations. 157 “ Review on the future of all forms of United Nations peace operations: report of the Secretary General ”, UN General Assembly A/80/798 – UN Security Council S/2026/600, 22 July 2026. The review came out in August, having originally been requested by member states in late 2024. Though this study covers political missions – and makes a strong pitch for the UN to reinvest in prevention and good offices, discussed in the next section – many of its more technical recommendations are specific to operations with military and police components. A number of UN members, including the U.S., have complained that it says nothing startlingly new. 158 See, for example, “ The future of United Nations peace operations: Implementation of the recommendations of the High-level Independent Panel on Peace Operations ”, UNGA A/70/357 – UNSC S/2015/682, 2 September 2015; “ Declaration of Shared Commitments on UN Peacekeeping Operations ”, UN Secretary-General, 16 August 2018; “ The Pact For The Future ”, UN General Assembly A/RES/79/1, 22 September 2024, paras 42(a)-42(g); “ Chair’s Summary – UN Peacekeeping Ministerial 2025 ”, 14 May 2025. UN missions face new challenges like disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks for which they are ill prepared. The report’s diagnosis of the problems facing peace operations is hard to dispute. As it notes, the UN is often tasked with propping up weak ceasefires and political processes amid endemic violence. UN missions face new challenges like disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks for which they are ill prepared. He suggests that the Security Council should direct UN operations to find political approaches to ending and mitigating conflict; work out “compacts” with states defining shared commitments to making missions work; and take a flexible approach to reviewing and revising mandates. His paper calls for a further Secretariat report examining the capabilities UN missions need to become more agile, while hammering home the need for missions to become more cost-effective and accountable for their performance. UN staffers and diplomats will spend much of the year ahead following up on these proposals, but even if they can fix some of the process issues, broader political questions about the future of UN peace operations will remain.
