UN officials agree that a high priority for the next Secretary-General is to sort out this option-generating and decision-making mess. Some believe it is a matter of a change in culture (and, in some cases, personnel). Others argue that it is necessary to centralise the UN’s systems for producing options and crisis coordination in a new planning cell inside the Secretary-General’s office, to speed up the process of responding to new conflicts and Security Council requests for help. The next Secretary-General would be well advised to resolve this top-level wiring issue – which will require fairly slight budgetary and managerial effort – before embarking on any wider reform of the Secretariat’s Departments of Peace Operations and Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, which will require more extensive inter-governmental negotiations, and more battles over turf. The new Secretary-General’s choice of senior officials dealing with peace and security will also come under scrutiny. The veto powers typically insist on inserting nominees to run significant departments, often as bargains during the final stages of choosing the Secretary-General. An unwritten division among the major powers has emerged: France fills the post of Under Secretary-General for Peace Operations, the U.S. takes political affairs, the UK deals with humanitarian affairs, China handles economic and social affairs, and Russia names the head of the Office of Counter-terrorism. UN officials and other member states grumble about this carve-up, but successive Secretaries-General have concluded that it is a political necessity to gain support from the Council’s permanent members. 166 Thant Myint-U, “ The Next Secretary-General, Secretariat Reform and the Vexed Question of Senior Appointments ”, NYU Center on International Cooperation, 11 April 2016. Some Secretariat staff worry that the Trump administration will lobby for a hardline loyalist to oversee the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, undermining the Secretary-General’s authority. While it may not be possible to ignore the veto powers entirely, however, both Guterres and his predecessor Ban Ki-moon were able to resist appointing nominees from Washington, Paris and London whom they deemed unsuitable. 167 Ben Donaldson and Fred Carver, “ Backroom Deals: The trade in promises for support between member states and candidates for UN Secretary-General ”, 1 for 8 Billion/Platforma CIPÓ, June 2026. To show at least a modicum of autonomy, the next Secretary-General should follow suit, potentially asking the veto powers for informal shortlists of candidates for particular roles. Equally or more importantly, she or he should look for strong appointees from non-veto capitals to fill key posts in the executive office – including Deputy Secretary-General, Chief of Staff and Political Director – who can buttress top-level decision-making and help balance the influence of P5 proxies in internal debates. 168 Daniel Safran-Hon, “ The Next Secretary-General’s First Decision: Who Runs the 38th Floor? ”, IPI Global Observatory, 13 May 2026. These senior officials could take on direct mediation roles as well. 169 Daniel Safran-Hon, “ UN Peacemaking Needs More Diplomats, Not More Doctrine ”, IPI Global Observatory, 26 August 2026. For all the qualities of her or his advisers, the Secretary-General will also need to get personally involved directly in conflict prevention efforts and peace processes. The new Secretary-General’s team will need to set up a series of early visits for the boss to key capitals in various regions so that she or he can signal that the UN is reinvesting in the business of conflict management. Whereas Guterres was discouraged by early failures in his peacemaking efforts, his successor should embrace a more persistent attitude toward the UN’s role in peacemaking. In the years ahead, the organisation’s biggest failure may not be to fall short of lofty expectations in crisis diplomacy, but to eschew engagement altogether. 170 Richard Gowan and Daniel Forti, “ Make the U.N. great again: The uphill struggle facing the next Secretary General ”, Time , 22 August 2026. IV. Conclusion The UN’s fortunes over the next twelve months will depend in no small part on who its members select as the next Secretary-General. She or he will face considerable pressure to hit the ground running and deliver quick wins for an organisation whose credibility has waned. Doing so will require the expenditure of limited political capital on a range of priorities. Member states will no doubt push the next UN chief to translate their vision for the organisation into plans for its peace and security, development and human rights pillars. The new Secretary-General will also be tasked with stabilising the organisation’s wobbling finances and spearheading a reform agenda. If the past year at the UN was defined by transition, then the coming year may be shaped by how quickly its new leader can deliver. But the next Secretary-General cannot mend all that is fraying at the UN without renewed support from its members. At a moment of worsening geopolitical competition, a more pragmatic approach may be for states to come to a more limited interpretation of the UN’s role in world affairs. Central to that vision would be the organisation’s potential as platform to reduce global risks through communication and deconfliction, rebuilding its credibility as a peacemaker, and helping alleviate the worst of civilian suffering. The organisation will surely also have a role to play in helping the most vulnerable weather global economic shocks, including those linked both to conflict (as in the case of a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz) and to other drivers (such as the El Niño climate pattern). Much of the debate about the UN’s work over the past year has centred on its shortcomings. That focus is understandable considering the worrying state of the international order. But as this briefing has shown, there are many crises where the UN is the only multilateral body with the mandate, legitimacy and capacity to open space for diplomacy. The organisation’s next leader would be wise to double down on those virtues. It may be an imperfect construction of the UN’s role in world affairs, but it is nonetheless an essential one.
